claims.text: The initial eutectic high-entropy alloy has dual-phase lamellar colonies containing internal boundaries prone to microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile deformation.
A trace boron addition will preferentially segregate to internal boundaries of the lamellar colonies.
Boron segregation will enhance interfacial cohesion and increase boundary cohesive energy.
Reinforcing the load-bearing interfaces will increase tensile strength.
Boundary reinforcement by the added solute will delay microcrack initiation and propagation during tensile deformation.
Suppressing microcrack initiation and propagation will improve tensile ductility.
Relative to the unmodified alloy, the boron-doped alloy will have both higher tensile strength and greater elongation at room temperature.
The unmodified lamellar alloy exhibits a strength-ductility trade-off associated with microcrack initiation at weak boundaries.
The boron concentration must be sufficiently low to promote boundary segregation without forming harmful secondary phases.
Formation of boron-associated secondary phases could compromise mechanical properties.
The magnitude of the strength and ductility improvements will depend on boron concentration, alloy composition, and processing parameters.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant simultaneous increase in both strength and ductility relative to an identically processed undoped control would falsify the hypothesis.
